draft_subject: ALD PhD framing across computation and health/society
draft_body:
Dear Daniels research-stream admissions team,

The ALD application connects four research areas and asks for three core-faculty preferences without requiring an advance commitment (https://www.daniels.utoronto.ca/doctor-philosophy-architecture-landscape-and-design-phd). That makes the programme a specific possibility for the enquiry I’m developing.

I’m preparing a PhD proposal for Proxy Society, an architecture research project on AI agents and robots acting for absent people under limited, revocable mandates. I would compare a library’s recessed proxy handoff with a shared staffed reception, using plans, sections and staged tests of expiry, revocation and human handoff. Personal arrival and staying remain available; the question is which spatial decision changes access and staff work.

Could you clarify how a proposal spanning computation and health/society should frame its three core-faculty preferences? I would also appreciate the appropriate route for confirming eligibility and whether a technical co-supervisor can support an architecture-led dissertation.

Best regards,
Kris Haamer
Proxy Society

draft_body:
Dear Toronto Society of Architects team,

Your Future-Ready Design Guide overview emphasizes durable early design decisions and stewardship (https://torontosocietyofarchitects.ca/future-ready-design-guide/). I’m interested in applying that attention to reversibility at a small civic threshold, while recognizing the guide’s housing focus.

I’m preparing a PhD proposal for Proxy Society, an architecture research project on AI agents and robots acting for absent people under limited, revocable mandates. A civic-building mock-up would compare a removable proxy service bay with a shared staffed waiting edge. Limited instructions would visibly expire or be revoked, and people could still arrive and stay. The comparison asks whether an adaptation can be removed when it weakens collective use.

Could you suggest a Toronto practitioner or researcher who could critique the reversibility and stewardship of that arrangement? A relevant public discussion or one focused introduction would help shape the doctoral proposal.

Best regards,
Kris Haamer

Dear TPL research team,

Your AI policy preserves human judgement and oversight in staff work (https://tpl.ca/policies-and-terms-of-use/artificial-intelligence-policy/). I’m seeking process guidance on a future spatial-research idea that would make a visitor’s delegated instruction similarly understandable.

I’m preparing a PhD proposal for Proxy Society, an architecture research project on AI agents and robots acting for absent people under limited, revocable mandates. An off-site mock-up would compare a library proxy pickup recess with a shared staffed counter, testing how people understand scope, expiry and cancellation while personal arrival remains available. A consent-based workshop could examine access and staff verification work.

Could you clarify whether this workshop approach could fit your research priorities if intake reopens, and which planning contact would be appropriate? I understand new requests are paused and observational research is prohibited; any future proposal would need the required institutional ethics and library review.

Kris Haamer
